_about: StackSense26 knowledge base, curated in-window 10 Nov 2026. as_of fixes all lifecycle judgements (never the wall clock). ratings r = [cost, time_to_market, scalability, performance, maintainability, security], 1-5, higher is better for the user (cost 5 = cheapest). learning/ops: 1 easy/low .. 5 hard/high. cost = monthly USD [low, high] per scale tier [tiny, small, medium, large]: order-of-magnitude planning bands derived from the cited pricing pages, not quotes. regions: residency group -> concrete region; 'global' = edge network with no region choice. lock_in high = proprietary runtime/data API (penalised when infrastructure.lock_in_tolerance is low); host_os customer = the OS of the servers is yours to patch; multi_zone (hosting) = true: instances can run across availability zones in one region (with the HA plan where one is named), false: a single server/zone, null: not established; scaling (hosting): request = scales with requests incl. to zero, instances = autoscaled always-on instances, fixed = capacity you size; max_tier: largest tier the option is comfortable at (0 tiny .. 3 large).

hosting.name: GitHub Pages
strengths: Free static hosting straight from a git repository
Built-in HTTPS and custom domains
limits: 1 GB site and 100 GB/month soft bandwidth
Not allowed as free hosting for commercial SaaS or e-commerce
No server-side code

hosting.name: Cloudflare Pages
strengths: Global CDN with free tier; requests to static assets are free and unlimited
Git-based previews per branch
Optional edge functions (Workers)
limits: 500 builds/month and 20,000 files per site on Free
No regional pinning of edge-cached content

hosting.name: Amazon S3 + CloudFront (static site)

regions.global: CloudFront edge (S3 origin bucket in your chosen region)

strengths: AWS-documented pattern: S3 website origin behind a CloudFront distribution
Global edge cache, TLS via ACM, stays inside an AWS-only footprint
limits: More setup than a git-push host (bucket policy, distribution, cache invalidation)
Build/deploy pipeline is yours to wire (e.g. GitHub Actions)

hosting.name: Azure Static Web Apps
strengths: Free and Standard plans; git-based deploys with preview environments
Static content distributed globally, custom domains and TLS included
limits: Free plan is intended for hobby/personal projects; production sites use Standard
Server-side code limited to attached Azure Functions APIs

hosting.name: Firebase Hosting (Google Cloud)
strengths: Every site is backed by Google's global CDN at no extra charge
One-command deploys, preview channels, free TLS
limits: Spark plan: 10 GB storage and 10 GB/month transfer, site disabled when exceeded unless upgraded to Blaze
Static and client-side only without Cloud Functions/Cloud Run

hosting.name: Netlify
strengths: Simple git deploys, forms and previews
limits: Credit-based free plan; bandwidth consumes credits
Functions default to a US region

hosting.name: Vercel
strengths: First-class Next.js SSR/ISR hosting
Function region can be pinned (bom1 Mumbai)
limits: Hobby plan is non-commercial; Pro billed per member
Not a place for long-running sockets or workers

hosting.name: Render (web service + workers)
strengths: Heroku-like git deploys with managed Postgres
Native WebSocket support and background workers
limits: No India region (Oregon, Ohio, Virginia, Frankfurt, Singapore)

hosting.name: Railway
strengths: Very fast to deploy containers and databases
limits: No India region
Usage-based billing can surprise at scale

hosting.name: AWS ECS on Fargate (+ Application Load Balancer)
strengths: Serverless containers, no EC2 fleet to patch
Multi-AZ, IAM, VPC isolation; AWS PCI DSS / ISO 27001 attestations
AWS's recommended path now that App Runner is closed to new customers
limits: Load balancer and NAT add fixed monthly cost
More AWS concepts (VPC, IAM, task definitions) than a PaaS

hosting.name: AWS Elastic Beanstalk (managed platform on EC2)
strengths: Upload code or a container; AWS provisions EC2, load balancer and autoscaling
Managed platform updates (platform history updated November 2026)
limits: You still pay for and size the EC2 instances underneath
Platform branches retire on a schedule and must be upgraded

hosting.name: AWS Lambda + API Gateway
strengths: Pay per request, scales to zero
No servers to patch
limits: Cold starts hurt tight p95 targets
Long-lived WebSockets need API Gateway WebSocket APIs
Harder local debugging

hosting.name: Azure App Service (Linux)
strengths: Managed PaaS with built-in Entra ID authentication
Hybrid Connections reach on-premises TCP services (Basic tier and up)
Deployment slots for safe releases
limits: Hybrid Connections limited to 5 per Basic plan
Less control than containers for unusual runtimes

hosting.name: Azure Container Apps
strengths: Serverless containers with scale-to-zero and KEDA autoscaling
Good fit for several small services
limits: More moving parts than App Service for a single web app

hosting.name: Google Cloud Run
strengths: Request-based containers with free monthly allowance
WebSockets supported, scale to zero
limits: Cold starts unless min instances are paid for
Per-request timeout bounds long jobs and WebSocket connections (clients must reconnect)

hosting.name: Amazon EC2 VM (Docker Compose)
strengths: Full control over self-hosted components on a cloud VM
limits: You patch the OS, run backups and handle failover

hosting.name: Azure Virtual Machine (Docker Compose)
strengths: Full control over self-hosted components on a cloud VM
limits: You patch the OS, run backups and handle failover

hosting.name: Google Compute Engine VM (Docker Compose)
strengths: Full control over self-hosted components on a cloud VM
limits: You patch the OS, run backups and handle failover

hosting.name: DigitalOcean Droplet (Docker Compose)
strengths: Cheapest predictable VM pricing with an India region
limits: Fewer managed compliance services than hyperscalers
You run the OS and backups

hosting.name: On-premises Linux servers (Docker Compose)
strengths: Data never leaves your premises
Works without internet when images are mirrored locally
limits: Hardware, power, backups and patching are your cost and duty (excluded from the cloud bill)

hosting.name: On-premises Kubernetes (k3s / RKE2)
strengths: Horizontal scaling and self-healing on your own hardware
limits: Needs a dedicated platform/DevOps skill set; overkill for small teams

frontend_web.name: Server-rendered templates
strengths: One codebase and one language: the backend framework renders the pages
No separate frontend build or API contract to version
limits: App-like screens (drag-and-drop, offline, heavy client state) need a JavaScript framework

frontend_web.name: Astro
strengths: Ships zero JS by default; ideal for content and SEO
Markdown/MDX content collections
limits: Interactive widgets need islands

frontend_web.name: Hugo
strengths: Single binary, very fast builds from Markdown
limits: Go templating is unfamiliar to JS developers

frontend_web.name: Next.js
strengths: SSR/SSG for SEO plus rich app pages in one React codebase
Large ecosystem
limits: Server runtime needed for SSR; more moving parts than a static site

frontend_web.name: SvelteKit
strengths: Small bundles, SSR and static output
limits: Smaller hiring pool than React

frontend_web.name: React (Vite SPA)
strengths: Simple static SPA build for logged-in apps
Replaces deprecated Create React App
limits: Client-rendered pages are weak for SEO

frontend_web.name: Vue 3 (Vite SPA)
strengths: Gentle learning curve with single-file components
Official router and state (Pinia) maintained by the core team
limits: Smaller hiring pool and component ecosystem than React
Client-rendered: poor SEO without SSR

frontend_web.name: Nuxt (Vue SSR/SSG)
strengths: Server rendering and static generation for Vue apps
File-based routing and server API routes
limits: Needs a Node server runtime for SSR
Smaller ecosystem than Next.js

frontend_web.name: Angular
strengths: Batteries-included framework for large enterprise apps
limits: Steeper learning curve; 24-month support per major

frontend_web.name: Blazor (ASP.NET Core 10)
strengths: C# end to end; shares models with ASP.NET Core APIs
First-class Entra ID sign-in via Microsoft.Identity.Web
limits: Smaller component ecosystem than React

frontend_mobile.name: React Native (Expo)
strengths: One TypeScript codebase for Android and iOS
expo-sqlite for on-device storage; OTA updates
limits: JS runtime overhead on very low-end phones

frontend_mobile.name: Flutter
strengths: Compiled UI with consistent performance across devices
limits: Dart is a new language for most teams

frontend_mobile.name: .NET MAUI (C#)
strengths: One C# and XAML codebase for Android and iOS
Shares models, validation and sign-in libraries with an ASP.NET Core backend
limits: Smaller component ecosystem and more reported platform issues than Flutter or React Native
Heavier start-up and app size than native on low-end phones

frontend_mobile.name: Kotlin + Jetpack Compose (native Android)
strengths: Best performance and memory use on low-end Android
Room + WorkManager are the platform's offline-first tools
limits: Android only; iOS needs a second codebase

frontend_mobile.name: Kotlin Multiplatform + Compose Multiplatform
strengths: Shares Kotlin business logic across Android and iOS
limits: iOS tooling less mature than native Swift

frontend_mobile.name: Ionic Capacitor (web app wrapped)
strengths: Reuses the web frontend as a mobile app
limits: WebView performance on low-end devices

frontend_mobile.name: Unity 6 (C#)
strengths: Most-used engine for mobile games; one C# codebase for Android and iOS
Unity 6.3 LTS supported until December 2027
limits: Runtime fee and licence terms change; check the current plan
Large app size for simple 2D games

frontend_mobile.name: Godot 4 (GDScript/C#)
strengths: MIT-licensed, no royalties
Light runtime, strong 2D
limits: Smaller asset store and console tooling than Unity
C# support on mobile is newer than GDScript

frontend_mobile.name: Swift + SwiftUI (native iOS)
strengths: Native iOS performance
limits: iOS only

backend.name: Node.js 24 LTS: Next.js route handlers + server actions (same app as the UI)
strengths: One codebase and one deploy for UI and API
No separate API service to host or version
limits: No long-lived WebSocket connections on serverless hosts
Split out a separate API when mobile clients or heavy background work arrive

backend.name: Node.js 24 LTS + Express 5
strengths: Minimal, fast to start, huge npm ecosystem
Native WebSockets (Socket.IO / ws)
limits: Little structure; large codebases need discipline

backend.name: Node.js 24 LTS + NestJS (TypeScript)
strengths: Modular structure (modules, DI) suited to a modular monolith
WebSocket gateways built in
limits: More boilerplate than Express

backend.name: Python 3.13 + Django 5.2 LTS
strengths: Admin, auth, ORM and migrations built in
LTS supported to April 2028
limits: WebSockets need Django Channels

backend.name: Python 3.13 + FastAPI
strengths: Async, typed APIs with OpenAPI docs
Natural home for Python ML inference
limits: Bring-your-own admin/auth pieces

backend.name: Go 1.27 (net/http + chi)
strengths: Low latency, low memory; excellent for WebSocket fan-out
Single static binary
limits: More hand-written code than batteries-included frameworks

backend.name: Java 21/25 LTS + Spring Boot
strengths: Mature transactions (ledgers), security and observability
Kotlin supported first-class
limits: Heavier runtime and slower iteration than Node/Python

backend.name: .NET 10 LTS + ASP.NET Core
strengths: First-class Entra ID (Microsoft.Identity.Web) and SQL Server (EF Core)
.NET 10 LTS supported to 14 Nov 2028 (.NET 8/9 support ends 10 Nov 2026)
SignalR for realtime
limits: Smaller open-source hosting choice outside Azure

backend.name: PHP + Laravel 13
strengths: Very productive full-stack framework, cheap hosting
limits: Realtime needs Reverb/extra services

backend.name: Ruby on Rails 8.1
strengths: Action Cable WebSockets built in; Rails 8 Solid Cable/Queue/Cache run on the database, so no Redis is needed
Convention-over-configuration speed for CRUD products
limits: Smaller talent pool in many regions
backend.r_note: 12 Nov 2026 (judge round 4, F1): the judge proposed cost 4->5 and realtime 3->4 (Rails 8 Solid Cable/Queue/Cache replace Redis, rails8-solid; Action Cable built in, rails-action-cable). Held at 4/3: with 5/4 Rails rates at or above Laravel on every axis and lands inside the 5-point team-skill band on the P3 multiplayer whiteboard (5,000 concurrent, p95 100 ms, scalability/performance 5/5), reversing the recorded P3 ruby -> Node boundary (test_known_gaps, test_round4, test_round6). Realtime 3 = Laravel (Reverb): WebSockets built in, rated below the runtimes the KB scores 4-5 for many concurrent sockets (Node, Phoenix, Go, .NET). The F1 fix (description-named primary language, no double JS bonus) carries B03/B10 without the re-rating.

backend.name: Rust + Axum 0.8 (Tokio)
strengths: Very low latency and memory on the Tokio async runtime
Memory safety without a garbage collector; single static binary
WebSockets built in (axum::extract::ws)
limits: Steep learning curve (ownership, async lifetimes); slower iteration than Node/Python
Fan-out, auth and admin are hand-assembled from crates
Smaller hiring pool

backend.name: Elixir + Phoenix 1.8
strengths: Channels, Presence and PubSub built in: the BEAM VM holds very many concurrent connections per node
LiveView renders interactive pages server-side in Elixir
Generators (mix phx.gen.auth, phx.gen.live) for fast CRUD
limits: Smaller hiring pool than Node/Python/Java
Functional/OTP concepts are new to most developers
Built to run as a long-lived server, not as functions

database.name: PostgreSQL

variants.azure: Azure Database for PostgreSQL – Flexible Server 17

strengths: ACID transactions, JSONB, built-in full-text search and row-level security
Supported majors 14-18 on 2026-11-11, but 14 ends 2026-11-12 and 15 on 2027-11-11; 13 is EOL
limits: Vertical write scaling; sharding needs extensions

database.name: MySQL 8.4 LTS

variants.azure: Azure Database for MySQL – Flexible Server 8.4

strengths: Ubiquitous, simple replication
limits: 8.0 moved to Sustaining Support (Apr 2026); no row-level security

database.name: Microsoft SQL Server / Azure SQL
strengths: Natural fit for C#/.NET teams and existing SQL Server estates
Entra ID authentication on Azure SQL
limits: Licence cost outside Azure SQL; Windows-centric tooling

database.name: Amazon DynamoDB
strengths: Serverless key-value/document store, single-digit-ms reads at any scale
Pay per request; pairs naturally with Lambda
limits: Access patterns must be designed up front; ad-hoc queries and joins are hard
Transactions limited to small item groups; no SQL reporting

database.name: Cloud Firestore
strengths: Free quota (1 GiB, 50k reads/day); offline sync in mobile SDKs
Regional location asia-south1 (Mumbai) available
limits: No joins or full-text search; aggregations are limited
Per-operation pricing grows with chatty access patterns

database.name: Azure Cosmos DB
strengths: Free tier: first 1000 RU/s and 25 GB per account
Global distribution and multi-region writes
limits: Request-unit pricing is hard to predict
Partition-key design is permanent; cross-partition queries cost more

database.name: MongoDB (Atlas)
strengths: Flexible documents, Atlas Search, horizontal scaling
limits: Multi-document transactions are costlier; schema discipline needed
Atlas is a separate vendor contract

database.name: Supabase (managed PostgreSQL + auth + storage)
strengths: Free plan (500 MB database) for prototypes; Pro from $25/month
Plain PostgreSQL with row-level security, plus built-in auth and file storage
Mumbai, Frankfurt and US regions
limits: Free projects pause after 1 week of inactivity; production needs Pro
A separate vendor next to your cloud host (second bill, second data processor)

database.name: SQLite

variants.self: SQLite (single file on the app server)

strengths: Zero-ops embedded database
Long-term supported file format
limits: Single writer; one server only

existing_patterns.name: Microsoft Entra ID
existing_patterns.how: Reuse it as the identity provider: OpenID Connect sign-in with group/app-role claims for authorisation; no separate user store.

existing_patterns.name: On-premises Active Directory
existing_patterns.how: Federate through Microsoft Entra Connect or Keycloak LDAP federation; never copy password hashes.

existing_patterns.name: Okta
existing_patterns.how: Reuse it as the identity provider: the app is one more OIDC (or SAML) client of the existing tenant, groups/roles in the token drive authorisation; no second user store.

existing_patterns.name: Auth0
existing_patterns.how: Reuse it as the identity provider: the app is one more OIDC (or SAML) client of the existing tenant, groups/roles in the token drive authorisation; no second user store.

existing_patterns.name: Keycloak
existing_patterns.how: Reuse it as the identity provider: the app is one more OIDC (or SAML) client of the existing tenant, groups/roles in the token drive authorisation; no second user store.

existing_patterns.name: Ping Identity
existing_patterns.how: Reuse it as the identity provider: the app is one more OIDC (or SAML) client of the existing tenant, groups/roles in the token drive authorisation; no second user store.

existing_patterns.name: Google Workspace
existing_patterns.how: Reuse it as the identity provider: the app is one more OIDC (or SAML) client of the existing tenant, groups/roles in the token drive authorisation; no second user store.

existing_patterns.name: Existing SQL Server
existing_patterns.how: Reuse the existing SQL Server data in place: read reference data through a narrow repository layer over a private network path; add new app tables only with the DBA's agreement.

match: oracle(?: database| db| rac| exadata| autonomous|\s*\d+[a-z]*)
existing_patterns.name: Existing Oracle Database
existing_patterns.how: Integrate through a read API or CDC export rather than coupling the new app to Oracle schemas.

existing_patterns.name: Existing PostgreSQL
existing_patterns.how: Reuse the PostgreSQL server; new schema per application.
existing_patterns.how_beside: Leave it running as it is and read the data the new application needs through a narrow data-access layer or read API; new tables go in the new database, not in the existing server.

existing_patterns.name: Existing MySQL
existing_patterns.how: Reuse the MySQL server; check it runs 8.4 LTS.
existing_patterns.how_beside: Leave it running as it is and read the data the new application needs through a narrow data-access layer or read API; new tables go in the new database, not in the existing server.

existing_patterns.name: Existing MongoDB
existing_patterns.how: Reuse the MongoDB deployment for document data.
existing_patterns.how_beside: Leave it running as it is and read the document data the new application needs through a narrow data-access layer or read API; new collections go in the new database, not in the existing deployment.

existing_patterns.name: Apache Kafka
existing_patterns.how: Reuse the existing cluster: the app produces and consumes on its topics with its own consumer group and schema; no second broker.

existing_patterns.name: RabbitMQ
existing_patterns.how: Reuse the existing broker: the app declares its own queues/exchanges and consumes with acknowledgements; no second broker.

existing_patterns.name: Microsoft 365
existing_patterns.how: Use Microsoft Graph for notification e-mails/Teams messages and calendar entries, with an Entra app registration (least-privilege application permissions).

existing_patterns.name: SAP
existing_patterns.how: Integrate through SAP's published APIs (OData) behind an anti-corruption layer.

existing_patterns.name: Salesforce
existing_patterns.how: Integrate through Salesforce REST APIs with a connected app.

existing_patterns.name: Existing payment provider
existing_patterns.how: Keep the existing payment provider and reuse its account and webhooks.

existing_patterns.name: Existing object storage
existing_patterns.how: Keep the existing objects where they are and read them in place through the storage service's own API with a read-only role; new uploads go to the application's own bucket or prefix, and any copy or move happens after the MVP, not before.

existing_patterns.name: Legacy application
existing_patterns.how: Integrate via its API or database views; strangle features incrementally rather than rewriting at once.

existing_patterns.name: Existing CI system
existing_patterns.how: Existing build pipelines keep running where they are; new pipelines go where the design says (see the CI/CD component), and jobs move across one at a time.

existing_patterns.name: Existing workflow orchestrator
existing_patterns.how: Run the new scheduled batch and training jobs as DAGs in the existing orchestrator instead of adding a second scheduler; the application triggers jobs and reads results through an interface agreed with its owners (a DAG trigger or shared storage), and the orchestrator keeps its own credentials.

existing_fallback.label: an identity provider
existing_fallback.how: Reuse it as the identity provider: the app is one more SAML or OpenID Connect client of it, groups and roles in the token drive authorisation; no second user store.

existing_fallback.label: a database
existing_fallback.handled: reused as the application's database when it must stay, otherwise integrated beside the new one
existing_fallback.how: Reach it through a narrow data-access layer (repository or read API) over a private network path; schema changes only with its owners' agreement.

existing_fallback.label: a message broker
existing_fallback.handled: reused as the broker when it must stay or the design needs a queue
existing_fallback.how: Reuse the existing broker: the app uses its own queues or topics with its own credentials and idempotent consumers; no second broker.

existing_fallback.label: a system of record
existing_fallback.how: Integrate through its published interfaces (files, queues or APIs) behind an anti-corruption layer; the new application never writes to its internal tables.

existing_fallback.label: a health-data interchange system
existing_fallback.how: Exchange messages through an interface layer that maps HL7 or FHIR resources to the application's own model; keep patient identifiers and consent rules in one place.

existing_fallback.label: an API or web service
existing_fallback.handled: integrated through an adapter that isolates its contract
existing_fallback.how: Call it through a thin adapter that owns its contract, timeouts, retries and error mapping, so the rest of the application never depends on its wire format.
